newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton warms up for round with "The Shark".
newsitem.headline: Clinton warms up for round with "The Shark".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, enjoying a working holiday in Australia, went jogging by Sydney Harbour on Thursday to prepare for a date with "The Shark" -- golfing champion Greg Norman.
"That's what this is all about," a panting Clinton said after a 20-minute run through Sydney's Royal Botanic Gardens when asked about teeing off with Norman later on Thursday.

On Wednesday, Clinton became only the second U.S. president to address both houses of the Australian parliament and used the occasion to deliver his first major foreign-policy speech since his November 5 re-election.
In it he reaffirmed Washington's military, political and economic commitment to the Asia-Pacific region and called for a deeper engagement with China.
"In a global economy with global security challenges America must look to the East no less than to the West," Clinton said.

Clinton is spending nine days in the Asia-Pacific region and the centrepiece of his trip is a meeting in Manila on Sunday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin and an APEC regional summit the following day.
But the final three days of Clinton's Australian visit are dedicated to sightseeing and leisure, with the highlight a round of golf with Australian world number one Norman on Thursday.
Clinton could have chosen to play young American star Tiger Woods, who is competing at the same Sydney tournament as Norman, but the choice of Norman is not without some political echo.
During his recent re-election campaign, while he was riding high in the polls over Republican Bob Dole, Clinton regularly told complacent aides: "Remember Greg Norman".
Known as a "choker", the world's greatest golfer went into the final round of April's U.S. Masters with a six-stroke lead only to lose by five strokes to Britain's Nick Faldo.
But before teeing off, Clinton was due to give a lunch-time speech on Thursday to the people of Australia from a cove in the shadow of the Sydney Opera House.

Aides said Clinton would use the speech to highlight the two countries' common democratic heritage and praise the idea of cultural diversity. That could be touching a raw nerve given Australia's recent national debate on race and immigration sparked by a maverick politician from Queensland.
Hillary Clinton is due to make her first speech of the trip when she addresses a select group of Australian women in the Sydney Opera House on the issue of women in the 21st century.
After his jog on Wednesday morning, Clinton made an impromtu visit to the landmark opera house, enlisting security guard Jim Samuel to give him a tour.

An opera house official soon rushed up and took over for Clinton's 20-minute walkabout. "It's like two different buildings. It's really quite amazing," Clinton said of the distinctive white sail-like roofs.
On Thursday evening, the Clintons fly to Australia's tropical north for two days at the Great Barrier Reef resort of Port Douglas. They will leave on Saturday for the Philippines.
The five-day Australia trip is designed to revitalise the president after his gruelling re-election campaign and Clinton has already begun collecting souvenirs from his holiday "Down Under".
Crocodile farmer and national politican Warren Entsch said Clinton had asked him for a pair of crocodile boots during Wednesday's lunch in parliament in Canberra.
"I don't suppose there would be too many crocodile farmers in houses of parliament around the world," Entsch said.
"To have a pair of...boots made from Australian crocodile skins on the presidential feet is not a bad trade coup for Australia."
